title: The Mountain Held Up by Sticks
tease: A seven-year-old holds a hill over a village for seven days. A cowherd puts his stick up to help.

source.traditionNote: Told the same way in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and the Harivaṃśa. This is one of the stable ones.

sourcing.claim: Vraja makes an annual offering to Indra at the end of the rains
Kṛṣṇa argues the offering should go to Govardhana, which gives grass, water and shade
The elders accept and the offering is redirected; the village circumambulates the hill
Indra sends destroying clouds; rain for seven days; cattle and people in danger
Kṛṣṇa lifts Govardhana on the little finger of his left hand and shelters them
The cowherds support the hill with their staves
After seven days Indra withdraws; Kṛṣṇa replaces the hill

blocks.text: «Kṛṣṇa» was seven when he asked the awkward question.

Every year the village of «Vraja» sent its harvest offering up to «Indra», king of the gods, who sends the rain. Kṛṣṇa said: _whose grass do our cows eat? Whose streams do we drink? Whose shade do we sit in? «Govardhana»'s. Why do we never thank the hill?_
So that year the offering went to «Govardhana». The village prepared food for the hill, honoured the cows, and walked around the mountain together.

«Indra» was not thanked, and he was furious. He sent destroying storm clouds over «Vraja». The rain came sideways, then kept coming until cattle stood in water up to their knees and roofs began to come apart.
The frightened villagers ran to «Kṛṣṇa». He was the one person who did not look afraid. The same boy who had redirected the offering now had to answer for the danger that followed.
He walked to «Govardhana», put one hand under its edge, and lifted the hill like a great roof. He held it on the little finger of his left hand and called the whole village underneath.
They came in: cows, calves, carts, children, elders, dogs, and everything they could bring out of the rain. Under the hill, the village had a dry place to stand together.

And one cowherd, looking up at a seven-year-old holding a mountain, thought: _he must be getting tired._ So he raised his stick and pressed it against the underside of the hill. To help. Their staves formed a ring under the hill. They believed they were sharing the weight.
The rain continued for seven days. The cowherds raised their own sticks against the underside of the hill to help. «Kṛṣṇa» let them help, and the whole village waited out the storm together.

«Kṛṣṇa» never laughed at them for trying to help. Their sticks were not carrying the mountain, but their desire to help still mattered. The mountain was in his hand, and the effort under it belonged to everyone.
Every year, when the rains were finishing, the people of «Vraja» made a great offering to «Indra», king of the gods, who sends the rain.

It took a month to get ready. The rice came in on carts. The butter was churned in the big pots and carried out in the cool of the morning, and the children were told not to touch it about four hundred times.
That year, a boy asked a question.

«Kṛṣṇa» was seven. He said: _whose grass do the cows eat? The mountain's. Whose water do we drink? The mountain's streams. Whose shade do we sit in all afternoon? «Govardhana»'s. So why do we never thank the mountain?_

The elders argued about it. «Indra» had been thanked for as long as anyone could remember, and nobody could say what would happen if the village stopped. «Kṛṣṇa» kept returning to the same question: what actually feeds the cows and people every day?
But the seven-year-old would not let the question go. The village finally agreed to make its offering to the hill that fed its cattle and gave them water and shade.

So that year the food went to Govardhana. Mountains of rice, hills of butter, whole trees of banana leaf. The whole village circumambulated «Govardhana», and the cows went too. The offering had moved from a distant god of rain to the hill, grass and water that sustained their daily life.
«Indra» was not thanked. He saw the redirected offering as an insult and responded with anger.
He sent the storm clouds meant to destroy the settlement. They came in low, black as wet stone, and the rain fell sideways without moving on.

It fell for a day, and then for two, and then the cattle were standing in water up to their knees, and the calves were being carried, and the children were crying, and the roofs were coming apart above them.
The frightened villagers ran to «Kṛṣṇa». He was the one person who did not look afraid. The same boy who had redirected the offering now had to answer for the danger that followed.
He walked out to «Govardhana» in the rain and put one hand under its edge. His answer was not another argument with «Indra»; it was shelter.
And he lifted the hill.

Govardhana came up out of the earth like a lid off a pot — the whole hill, with its trees and its goat paths and its streams still running down the sides of it — and he held it over the village on the little finger of his left hand, and he said, _come in._

They came in: cows, calves, carts, children, elders, dogs, and the things they had managed to carry. Under the hill they had shelter from the rain. The village that had been scattered by the storm now stood together with its cattle in one dry place.
They looked up at a seven-year-old holding a mountain and decided he must be getting tired. The thought was completely reasonable from where they were standing.
So one cowherd lifted his stick and pressed it against the underside of the mountain to help. Then another copied him, and soon many of them were doing the same.
Their staves formed a ring under the hill. They believed they were sharing the weight.

For seven days the rain continued. The cowherds stood with their sticks against the underside of the hill, helping in the only way they could. «Kṛṣṇa» did not tell them their sticks were unnecessary. He let their help remain part of the shelter.
When «Indra» finally withdrew the storm, «Kṛṣṇa» waited until the people and cattle had come out from underneath. Only then did he lower «Govardhana» back into its place.
«Kṛṣṇa» never laughed at the cowherds for trying to help.
The mountain was in his hand, but their desire to help still had a place under it. That is why the little staves matter.

linked.reason: another story about help that looks too small to matter

close.question: Kṛṣṇa could have said, _put your sticks down, I've got it._ Why do you think he didn't?
close.seed: Letting someone help you is its own kind of kindness.

ifTheyAsk.a: No — and it is worth saying so out loud. Indra was used to being thanked, and he stopped checking whether he had earned it. That is not a monster; that is a very ordinary way for a powerful person to go wrong. Children recognise it immediately, usually in a grown-up they know.

ifTheyAsk.q: Could a boy really lift a mountain?
ifTheyAsk.a: In the story, yes, and the story is not trying to be a report. What it is doing is putting a very large thing and a very small person in the same picture so you notice the difference. You can ask them back: what is the heaviest thing someone has ever carried for you?
